# Auth config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/auth/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.AuthBlock` configuring the near-side authentication the listeners front. **The attribute table below is the enumeration** — this sentence does not repeat it, because a prose copy of it has already gone stale here once. Each authenticator block names a way an arriving caller may prove who it is; the `chain` attribute names the ones to try, in evaluation order, and `rate_limit` bounds attempts across the chain.

**Not every block here is an authenticator, and the ones that are not say so.** `public {}` declares that a webhook listener has NO near-side authenticator because its producers sign their bodies instead (ADR-044 #1279) — it is legal only on a listener and refused on the global block. `issuer {}` declares that this deployment mints its own tokens and fronts its own login (ADR-135), which is the opposite direction from verifying somebody else's — it is legal only on the global block and refused on a listener, since one deployment has one issuer however many doors it opens, and it is where a deployment declares the remote identity providers its people log in through (`identity_provider "<name>" { oidc {} }`, ADR-135 D2/D12 — an edit to that set reaches the running issuer without a restart, unlike the `public_url` and `enabled` beside it). A block that judges no arriving caller does not count toward the `server`-profile gate that refuses to serve a client-facing listener with no authenticator: a vault whose only `auth` content is an issuer has declared no near-side authentication, since an issuer mints tokens and judges nobody. The tokens it mints need no authenticator block of their own — this daemon recognises what it signed, in process and against its own live signing keys (ADR-135 D7). Do not add a `jwt` block pointing at your own deployment: that attribute names an issuer this daemon TRUSTS, and aiming it here would admit, as the subject each names, every kind of token this daemon signs — including the ones its own authenticators refuse. It is refused: at load, a `jwt` block with no `audience` whose `issuer` or `jwks_url` names this deployment's issuer; and at key resolution, any token signed by this daemon's own keys, however a `jwt` block reached them.

A name `pkg/auth` implements that is NOT reachable from this block: a webhook authenticator. Chaining is likewise not a block — it is the `chain` attribute.

A singleton kind: the kind itself is the identity, and the composed result is one `auth` block for the whole vault — a second file declaring the same authenticator name is a merge conflict.

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `config/auth` |
| Regime | persisted |
| Identity regime | `singleton` — the kind itself is the identity; neither the stem nor a label carries meaning (ADR-087 D3) |
| Current version | `v1` |
| Supported versions | `v1` |
| HCL block | `auth` |
| Loader directory | `.tera/auth/<name>.hcl` |
| Go source | `github.com/kottera/kottera/pkg/config.AuthBlock` |
| Served at | `GET /api/v1/schemas/config/auth/reference` |

## Example

A minimal `auth`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/auth/example-auth.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

auth {
  static "example" {
    api_key "example" {
      key_hash = "8a7347045a068a4f6975445e94bbcd5247c269dea003fb72f6c3cc2e68c18092"
    }
  }
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `chain` | string[] | no | — | — | — | — |
| `jwt` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | — |
| `static` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | — |
| `file` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | — |
| `mtls` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | — |
| `introspection` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | — |
| `rate_limit` | block | no | — | — | — | — |
| `public` | block | no | — | PLAN-2026-09 Wave 3 | — | Declares that this listener has NO near-side authenticator, because its producers authenticate by SIGNING their bodies rather than by presenting a credential. Valid only on a webhook listener: it is refused on the global auth block (where it would mean this deployment authenticates nobody), on any other protocol (none of which has a signing convention to stand in for a credential), and beside any authenticator method in the same block. It is NOT a blanket allow — a public listener is refused at load unless EVERY webhook endpoint declares verify_signature, so the signature is the authentication rather than an absence of one, and an endpoint that verifies nothing cannot be reached through a public door. Note that the last check spans the whole endpoint set rather than this listener's share of it, because the webhook server serves one endpoint set on every webhook socket. Write it when a GitHub, Stripe or Slack producer must reach this daemon: such a producer has no way to send an Authorization header (ADR-044 #1279), and without this block it is answered 401 before its signature is ever read. |
| `issuer` | block | no | — | ADR-135 (PLAN-2026-09 the near-side issuer, Wave 1) | — | Declares that this deployment IS an OAuth issuer: the daemon mints its own tokens and fronts its own login page, so a person signs in to tera once and every plane — the MCP gateway, the management API and the CLI — sees that one identity (ADR-135 D1/D7). Do not confuse it with the jwt authenticator's own issuer attribute, which is a word away and points the other way: that names an issuer this daemon TRUSTS, while this block says this daemon BECOMES one. Valid only on the global auth block — a listener-level one is refused, because one deployment has one issuer and a listener declaring its own would declare a second issuer for one door. It declares no authenticator: an inbound credential is still judged by the authenticator blocks beside it, and a deployment that declares only this block has declared no near-side authentication. |
| `plugin_evidence` | block | no | — | PLAN-2026-09 plugins Wave 8 | — | The evidence classes a plugin's inbound submission may rest on anywhere in this deployment (ADR-141 D11): verified, evidence tera checked itself, and asserted, the plugin's word. ABSENT ACCEPTS BOTH, so a deployment that writes nothing behaves as D11 says; accept = ["verified"] forbids asserted everywhere, without touching a plugin that already sends raw signed requests. An installation may narrow its own policy with accept_evidence on its vouching grant and never widen past this one: config plan refuses an installation it installs or changes whose accept_evidence names a class this block does not accept (plugin_evidence_widened), and what a submission may rest on is always the intersection of the two. Valid only on the global auth block — a listener-level one is refused, because an inbound submission arrives on the plugin's socket or under its own token and never through a listener's authenticator chain. It declares no authenticator. Hot-reloadable: an edit reaches the next decision without a restart. |

## `jwt` block

Repeatable.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | — |
| `jwks_url` | string | no | — | — | — | The JWKS URL of the identity provider whose tokens this block accepts. Set it or issuer. It must name somebody else's key set: on a deployment running the near-side issuer, a block with no audience whose jwks_url names that issuer is refused at load, and a token signed by one of this daemon's own keys is refused through any jwt block, compared by key material, however the URL reached them. This daemon's own tokens are verified by its issuer and need no jwt block. |
| `issuer` | string | no | — | — | — | The issuer of the tokens this block accepts: checked against each token's iss claim, and, with no jwks_url, the URL OIDC discovery finds the key set from. It names an issuer this daemon TRUSTS, never this deployment's own: on a deployment running the near-side issuer, a block with no audience whose issuer names that issuer is refused at load (point the block at the external IdP it was meant for, or give it an audience). |
| `audience` | string | no | — | — | — | The aud claim every token must carry. Unset means aud is not checked, so a block with no audience admits any token its key set verifies. Setting one is the load-time repair for a block that names this deployment's own issuer, though tokens signed by this daemon's keys are refused through it either way. |
| `groups_claim` | string | no | — | — | — | — |

## `issuer` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `public_url` | string | no | — | ADR-135 (PLAN-2026-09 the near-side issuer, Wave 1) | — | The issuer identity to publish when it differs from the address the gateway listener binds — the value that ends up in the iss claim of every token minted here, in the metadata document clients discover, and in the federated callback URL an operator registers at an identity provider. Unset means the address of the first mcp listener carrying this deployment's global near-side chain, which is where the issuer surface is served at all (ADR-135 Amendment 1): a listener declaring its own auth block serves no issuer route, so its address is never the fallback and a deployment with no other mcp listener is refused at load. The fallback is right for a daemon reached directly and wrong for one behind a reverse proxy or a tunnel, where clients would be handed an identity they cannot reach. Changing it is NOT hot-reloadable (ADR-122 D2, trust posture): tokens already in flight carry the old value, so the reload applies the rest and announces config.restart_required for this. |
| `enabled` | boolean | no | — | ADR-135 D10 (PLAN-2026-09 the near-side issuer, Wave 1) | — | Whether this deployment is an issuer. Tri-state. Unset means the deployment profile decides: on under server (and its gateway spelling), off under embedded and dev — so an operator who wants an issuer on a desktop daemon says so, and a gateway gets one without asking. true is an assertion that holds whatever the profile says. false is the off switch and wins under every profile, so turning the issuer off does not mean deleting the block and losing what is configured in it. Changing it is NOT hot-reloadable (ADR-122 D2 Amendment 4, trust posture): the issuer and its routes are built once at startup, so the reload applies the rest of the auth block, announces config.restart_required for this, and leaves the deployment an issuer (or not) exactly as it booted until you restart it. Adding or removing the issuer {} block itself is the same change by another spelling and is classified the same way. |
| `identity_provider` | block (list) | no | — | ADR-135 (PLAN-2026-09 the near-side issuer, Wave 2) | — | Zero or more remote identity providers this deployment federates logins to (ADR-135 D2/D12). The label is a reference name: it is what a user recipe's identity block names and how the audit trail identifies the provider, and two blocks sharing one label are refused at load naming the duplicate. Each block carries the provider-agnostic policy — allowed_domains and groups — and exactly one protocol block, which today is oidc {}. Hot-reloadable: adding, editing or removing a provider reaches the running issuer without a restart, and is reported applied rather than announcing config.restart_required (ADR-122 D1). The email_code block beside it reloads the same way; public_url and enabled stay restart-required, so a mixed edit applies the reloadable half and announces the rest. |
| `email_code` | block | no | — | ADR-172 D11 (PLAN-2026-10 guest access, Wave 1) | — | The email-code door: a sign-in that mails a six-digit code to the address a person types (ADR-172). Optional, and its absence is the golden path — with the email service configured and no email_code block the door is on and serves guests and invitations, which is what a deployment that configured email and lets people share needs. Declare it to admit members as well (admit_members) or to turn the door off without deleting what is configured beside it (enabled). Without the email service the door is off whatever this block says, and tera config plan warns that a declared email_code has nothing to send through. Hot-reloadable: an edit reaches the running issuer without a restart (ADR-122 D1). The code's length, lifetime and attempt ceiling have no attribute, and its send rates are admission { signin { code_sends_per_minute, code_sends_per_hour } }. |
| `browser_face` | block | no | — | ADR-182 D1 (PLAN-2026-10 browser face, Wave 1) | — | The browser face (ADR-182): the origin a person's browser is sent to for sign-in, consent and their own pages, served by a listener "browser" of its own, while public_url stays the identity agents, clients and dispatches use. Its presence is the declaration; absent, the deployment has one face, exactly as before. It comes with exactly one listener "browser": either without the other is refused at load. The face serves the issuer's browser routes and nothing an agent needs — not /mcp, not the token, registration or revocation endpoints, not the metadata documents — and accepts no presented credential. Not hot-reloadable (ADR-122 D2, trust posture, classified with public_url): its arrival, departure or any change announces config.restart_required. |
| `guests` | block | no | — | ADR-171 D14 (PLAN-2026-10 guest shares, Wave 1) | — | The guests' configuration (ADR-171 D14): how long an operator invitation stays pending (invitation_expiry, default 14d) and how long an ended guest's record is kept (retention, default 90d). Optional, and its absence is the golden path: absent, both defaults apply. There is no enable switch — every way a guest arrives is already an explicit decision, a share an installation permits or an invitation only an admin-granted ability makes. Valid only here, on the global auth block's issuer; a listener-level one is refused. Hot-reloadable: both values are read at use, so an edit reaches the next operator invitation and the guest janitor's next cycle and is reported applied, not restart-required (ADR-122 D1). The 14-day idle window after which a guest's sign-in lapses is a token lifetime, not configurable here. |

## `issuer.identity_provider` block

Nested under `issuer`. Repeatable.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | — |
| `allowed_domains` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Email domains whose people are provisioned a tera user record on their first login through this provider (ADR-135 D12). ABSENT OR EMPTY MEANS NOBODY — it is default deny, not an open door: a person outside the list is refused, gets no record, and the refusal is audited, while an admin may still admit them individually with a user recipe. Write the bare domain, not a pattern and not an address: example.com matches every address at that domain. A blank or whitespace-only entry is refused at load, because it would read as a domain that matches nothing while looking like a declaration that matches something. |
| `groups` | string[] | no | — | — | — | Groups every person who logs in through this provider receives (ADR-135 D6), merged with whatever groups the provider itself sends. It is the one place to grant a whole provider's people a baseline that works even when the provider returns no groups at all, which is the ordinary case for a consumer-grade one. Nothing here stamps a group onto a live identity by itself: per ADR-116 D1 groups reach a token only through the authentication event the login is. |
| `oidc` | block | no | — | — | — | OpenID Connect settings for this provider. Exactly one protocol block must be declared, and oidc is the only one this version defines — a provider with none is refused at load. Everything inside it is meaningful only under OpenID Connect, which is why it is a block rather than four attributes on the provider (ADR-087 section 3). |

**Exactly one of** `oidc`.

## `issuer.identity_provider.oidc` block

Nested under `issuer.identity_provider`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `discovery_url` | string | yes | — | — | — | The provider's issuer URL — the base the OpenID Connect discovery document is read from, so that the authorization, token and JWKS endpoints are learned from the provider rather than written here. Write the issuer itself (https://accounts.google.com), not the .well-known path: the discovery suffix is appended by the client that fetches it. |
| `client_id` | string | yes | — | — | — | This deployment's client id at the provider, as issued when tera was registered there. Registering tera as a client at a real provider is an operator act that no configuration can perform (ADR-135 D22), so this value is copied from the provider's own console. |
| `client_secret` | string | no | — | — | — | A CREDENTIAL REFERENCE to this deployment's client secret at the provider — keychain://name, env://VAR, vault://path or secret://name — and never the secret itself. This block is authored in a vault file and a vault is a git tree, so a literal here is committed and readable by everyone who can read the repository, which is why a bare literal is refused on every deployment profile but dev (where it warns). Write literal://value if you genuinely mean an inline value. Omit it entirely for a provider that issues none, which is what a public client with PKCE and no secret is. |
| `groups_claim` | string | no | — | — | — | The id-token claim this provider carries the person's groups in (groups is the usual spelling; an enterprise provider may use something else). Unset means the provider is not read for groups at all, and a person's groups are then whatever the provider block's own groups attribute grants them. Named here rather than beside that attribute because a claim name is meaningful only under OpenID Connect. |

## `issuer.email_code` block

Nested under `issuer`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | boolean | no | `true` | ADR-172 D11 (PLAN-2026-10 guest access, Wave 1) | — | Whether the email-code door is on. Default true. false turns the door off on a deployment that uses email only for correspondence and admits nobody by invitation, without deleting the block and what is configured in it. true does not turn the door on without the email service: with no email service configured the door is off whatever this says. |
| `admit_members` | boolean | no | `false` | ADR-172 D11 (PLAN-2026-10 guest access, Wave 1) | — | Who the door admits. Default false: guests and people holding an invitation only. true also admits any member whose address is verified, by ADR-172 D6's rules, so a member may sign in by a mailed code instead of a password or an identity provider. Narrowing it takes effect at the next request and the next right code: a member part-way through a code when it is turned off is refused at the code. |

## `issuer.browser_face` block

Nested under `issuer`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | string | yes | — | ADR-182 D1 (PLAN-2026-10 browser face, Wave 1) | — | The browser face's origin: where a person's browser is sent to sign in, served by the deployment's listener "browser" (ADR-182 D1). A bare origin — scheme, host and an optional port, with no path, query or fragment. https, or plain http only when the host is localhost. It is not the issuer's identity: public_url keeps the iss and aud of every token, the metadata documents and the token, registration and revocation endpoints, none of which the face serves. Changing it is NOT hot-reloadable (ADR-122 D2, trust posture): the reload applies the rest and announces config.restart_required. |
| `doors` | string[] | no | — | ADR-182 D7 (PLAN-2026-10 browser face, Wave 1) | — | The sign-in doors the face serves, in the words a session records the door that opened it by: passkey, provider, email_code and password (ADR-182 D7, ADR-173 D4). Unset is ["passkey", "provider", "email_code"]: the password door is served on the face only when listed. A door not listed answers 404 on the face. Listing a door this deployment has not configured is refused at load — provider with no identity_provider, email_code with the door off or no email service, passkey at a face URL whose host is an IP address. Step-up is not a sign-in door, and its methods are unaffected. tera config plan refuses a list that would leave a member with no way to sign in (ADR-171 D13). Not hot-reloadable, like url. |

## `issuer.guests` block

Nested under `issuer`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `invitation_expiry` | string | no | `14d` | ADR-171 D14 (PLAN-2026-10 guest shares, Wave 1) | — | How long an operator invitation stays pending before it expires unaccepted (duration; Nd for whole days, e.g. 14d, plus the usual h/m/s). Default 14d. Must be positive. It governs an invitation an operator made only: an invitation a share made expires with its share and ignores this. Read at use, so an edit reaches the next operator invitation without a restart; an invitation already pending keeps the expiry it was made with. |
| `retention` | string | no | `90d` | ADR-171 D14 (PLAN-2026-10 guest shares, Wave 1) | — | How long an ended guest's record is kept before it is deleted (duration; Nd for whole days, e.g. 90d, plus the usual h/m/s). Default 90d. Must be positive. A re-invitation within it revives the same record and id; after it, a new one is minted. Read at the janitor's next cycle, so an edit takes effect without a restart — and a shorter retention deletes, at that cycle, every ended guest already past it; tera config plan says how many. The ledger of who was a guest and who invited them outlives the deletion. |

## `plugin_evidence` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `accept` | string[] | yes | — | — | — | The evidence classes an inbound submission may rest on anywhere in this deployment, from verified (a raw request tera verified itself under the manifest's scheme with the installation's tera-audience secret) and asserted (the plugin's word). Required when the block is written. A member outside that vocabulary is refused at load, naming it. An EMPTY list is refused too: it would read as unset to one reader and as accept-nothing to another, and a deployment that wants no plugin to act for anyone declines the vouching grants instead. Repeating a member is harmless. An installation narrows its own policy with accept_evidence on its vouching grant, and the plan refuses one that names a class this list does not accept. |
